children.text: This is the San Lorenzo Martir parish church in Balangiga, Eastern Samar, the setting of the Balangiga incident of September 28, 1901. The three bells that the US Army took away returned in December 2018 and are now said to be at this church.

Balangiga is a municipality in Eastern Samar on the southern coast of Samar Island, facing Leyte Gulf. It sits at the mouth of the Balangiga River and neighbors Lawaan to the west, Llorente to the north, and Quinapondan and Giporlos to the east. The coordinates given on English Wikipedia are 11°6′33″N, 125°23′11″E; the 2024 population was 14,473 and the area is about 190.05 square kilometers. The parish's patron saint is St. Lawrence (San Lorenzo), Deacon and Martyr, whose feast day is August 10. It belongs to the Diocese of Borongan.

The church is famous because of the events of September 28, 1901. On that morning, during the Philippine–American War, villagers and Philippine revolutionary forces surprised Company C of the US 9th Infantry Regiment, which was occupying the town. English Wikipedia names Captain Eugenio Daza as the planner of the attack and police chief Valeriano Abanador as the man who led it. Abanador seized a sentry's rifle and struck him, which was the signal; church bells were rung and conch shells were blown.

The size of the company is given as 74 or 78 men depending on the source, and the death toll also varies, with figures of 36, 48, and 54 in total. Three American officers were killed, and the survivors escaped by sea to Basey and to Tanauan in Leyte. The townspeople captured about 100 rifles and 25,000 rounds of ammunition. Wikipedia describes the incident as the worst defeat of US Army soldiers since Little Bighorn in 1876. General Jacob H. Smith is recorded as then ordering Samar turned into a howling wilderness, and for that reason some Filipino historians use the name Balangiga massacre for this reprisal instead.

The church bells are the other protagonist of this story. The US Army took three bells as war trophies, and for more than a century they were kept at US military sites in Wyoming and in Korea. On July 24, 2017, President Duterte demanded their return in his State of the Nation Address; the bells arrived in Manila on December 11, 2018, and after a formal turnover ceremony on December 15 they returned that afternoon to the San Lorenzo Martir church. They rang in this church for the first time since 1901 at the dawn Mass on December 16. The bells can reportedly be seen at the church today. There are three bells. The 1853 bell bears the Franciscan coat of arms, the 1889 bell is inscribed with the name of Fr. Agustín Delgado, and the 1895 bell, said to have been the signal for the attack, is inscribed with the name of Fr. Bernardo Aparicio. The two larger bells were at Francis E. Warren Air Force Base (the former Fort D.A. Russell) in Wyoming, and the smallest signal bell was at Camp Red Cloud in Korea. Defense Secretary Jim Mattis certified the transfer on August 9, 2018, the return was announced on November 14, and the bells passed through Kadena Air Base in Japan before reaching Villamor Air Base in Manila on December 11. Some descendants of the Daza family, however, dispute this account, claiming for example that some of the Wyoming bells came from other churches.

Records say that an attack group hidden inside the church stormed the parish house and killed three officers. The Filipino and American accounts of this event differ, so rather than accept one side's version, we recommend reading several sources together.

The patron saint is St. Lawrence, Deacon and Martyr, and the feast day is August 10. It belongs to the Diocese of Borongan. The church and plaza are the center of the town, so after seeing the church it is good to walk around the plaza and imagine the layout at the time of the incident.
English Wikipedia notes that Balangiga has a statue and historical marker of Valeriano Abanador. Check its location on site.

blocks.title: The days of the December 2018 return

children.text: The sequence was arrival at Villamor Air Base in Manila on December 11, an airlift to Guiuan on the 14th and then overland to Balangiga, the turnover on the 15th, and the ringing of a bell at the dawn Mass on the 16th. Knowing these dates changes the way you look at the bells.

Wikivoyage says a commemoration with a reenactment is held in Balangiga every September 24, but the incident is known to have occurred on September 28, so the two dates differ. If you plan to visit, confirm the timing and content of the event first with the town hall or the church.

According to Wikipedia, Company C arrived on August 11, 1901 to close the port, and around mid-September Captain Thomas Connell reportedly held male residents overnight without food and confiscated bolos and stored rice. This pressure is cited as part of the background to the uprising.

blocks.title: The procession in disguise with coffins

children.text: Wikipedia describes how, a few hours before the attack, about 34 men from the village of Lawaan entered toward the church dressed as women worshippers, carrying small coffins that hid bolos and other weapons. A soldier is said to have opened one coffin, seen a child's body, and let the group pass. This scene is often cited in accounts of the incident.
At Tacloban’s Abucay terminal or another local pickup point, ask whether the Guiuan-bound van stops in Balangiga. Confirm the drop-off point and your segment fare at the counter before boarding.
When you arrive in Balangiga town, get off in front of the church and plaza. Walk around the church façade and bell tower from outside.
Look for the returned bells on the grounds of San Lorenzo de Martir Parish Church. For the church interior, check Mass times and follow the photography rules.
Have lunch in town and walk around the plaza. Ask locals where the Abanador statue and historical marker are.
Within town you can use tricycles, potpot (pedicabs), and motorcycle taxis (habal-habal). Check the time of the last vehicle back before you move on.
Check the time of the last return trip locally.

items.title: A history-reading route
items.subtitle: In order, inside and outside the church

children.text: In front of the church, picture the morning of September 28, 1901. The signal is said to have come between 6:20 and 6:45.
Inside the church, look at the three bells and compare the markings of the 1853, 1889, and 1895 bells.
Around the plaza, find the Abanador statue and historical marker and read the wording that explains the event from the Philippine side.
Walk out to the coast, look at the sea, and think about the route the survivors took when they escaped to Basey and Tanauan.
In front of the bells, also recall that the bells rang in this church for the first time since 1901 at the dawn Mass on December 16, 2018.
A flight from Manila to Tacloban (TAC) is the most practical way.

Balangiga local transport guide
describes Guiuan-bound Duptours vans that pass through town. In September 2026 the fare to the Guiuan terminus was listed at
one way. Ask separately about the fare to Balangiga.
Within the town, you are said to be able to take potpot, tricycles, and habal-habal.
The area around the church looks walkable, but check the exact route locally.

Balangiga is on the Pacific side of Samar and is affected by typhoons and the rainy season. A church visit is possible all year, but the journey is long, so you need to allow for weather. March to May is relatively dry.
August 10 is the parish patron saint's feast day, and a commemoration of the incident is said to be held in late September. Check the dates and content first with the town hall or the church.

We could not confirm lodging and restaurant information for Balangiga in the sources we opened. Cities such as Borongan and Guiuan are nearby, so if you need to stay overnight you can consider them as candidates, but weigh the travel time as well.
Bring snacks from Tacloban or buy them in Balangiga. The
Eastern Samar provincial business directory
lists Breadpoint Bakeshop and Belen’s Mini Mart in Poblacion 3. Check opening hours locally.
The church is a place of worship, so keep quiet during Mass and prayer.
Dress modestly and take photos in front of the bells in a respectful manner.
The Filipino and American accounts of the incident differ, so read several sources before you go and compare them with the explanation you hear locally.
The
Balangiga Bells visitor listing
gives free viewing at the plaza display. For a day trip, check the return van pickup point and last departure first.
Bring plenty of cash in pesos. Check in advance whether there is an ATM in town.
Ask the church or town hall before your visit about opening hours and the rules for viewing the bells.

There is a record that President Duterte himself rang a bell at the turnover ceremony on December 15, 2018, so reading photos and articles from that day beforehand will help you see the place much more clearly.
The date and casualty figures of the incident differ from source to source. Give priority to local explanations and the official markers.
